Still Marco Polo Airport wore me out, I slept in a plastic chair, took the water taxi. Early, too early the voices of children Mimicking the clatter in the Internet café In Campo Santo Stefano in a place of black coffee Bordellos of verse, bony accolades of joy, Saint Stephen stooped over a cross, A dog licking his heel, blood drops from a sign By the church wall—Anarchia è ordine— The refugee from Istria gathers up nails. She will cobble together a gondola with bits of driftwood Cast off the shores of the hunger-bitten Adriatic. In wind off the lagoon, A child hops in numbered squares, back and forth, back and forth, Cap on his head, rhymes cool as bone in his mouth. Whose child is he? No one will answer me. prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: And, The, Still

outputs.L1:
In the dog days of summer,  
as muslin curls in its own heat  
and crickets cry in the black walnut tree,  
the wind lifts up my life  
and sets it some distance from where it was.

Still, Marco Polo Airport wore me out.  
I slept in a plastic chair, then took the water taxi.  
Early—too early—the voices of children  
mimicked the clatter of the Internet café  
in Campo Santo Stefano, in a place of black coffee,  
bordellos of verse, bony accolades of joy.

Saint Stephen stooped over a cross,  
a dog licking his heel; drops of blood fell from a sign  
by the church wall—*Anarchia è ordine.*

The refugee from Istria gathers up nails.  
She will cobble together a gondola from bits of driftwood  
cast off the shores of the hunger-bitten Adriatic.

In the wind off the lagoon,  
a child hops through numbered squares,  
back and forth, back and forth,  
a cap on his head, rhymes cool as bone in his mouth.

Whose child is he?  
No one will answer me.

Voices from the music academy pour into sunlight  
that strikes the malarial wealth of empire:  
dreams of an old man in terrible heat,  
his hands bound with coarse cloth, tethered to a scaffold,  
still painting waves on the walls of the Palazzo Ducale.
outputs.L2:
At summer’s fiercest point, muslin twists in the heat it holds, while crickets call from the black walnut. A gust takes hold of my life and carries it away from its former place.

Even so, Marco Polo Airport exhausted me. I dozed in a molded-plastic seat before boarding the water taxi. At an unbearably early hour, children’s voices echoed the clicking and commotion of the Internet café in Campo Santo Stefano—a world of dark coffee, poetry’s brothels, and gaunt tributes to happiness. Saint Stephen bent above a cross. A dog lapped at his heel. Beside the church, drops of blood marked a sign declaring, *Anarchia è ordine*.

The Istrian refugee collects nails. Using scraps of driftwood thrown up along the coasts of the famine-ravaged Adriatic, she intends to piece together a gondola. In the breeze sweeping off the lagoon, a boy jumps repeatedly through numbered boxes. He wears a cap, and the rhymes on his tongue feel cold as bone. I ask who he belongs to, but no one replies.

Singing from the music academy spills into the daylight. The sun illuminates the empire’s fever-stricken riches and the visions of an old man suffering in brutal heat: his hands tied in rough fabric, his body fastened to scaffolding, yet still he paints waves across the walls of the Palazzo Ducale.
outputs.L3:
In the oppressive heat of summer, the wind seems to wrench the speaker’s life from its familiar course, carrying it toward uncertainty. Exhausted upon arriving at Marco Polo Airport, the speaker leaves solid ground behind and enters Venice by water taxi, crossing the lagoon in a dazed transition between travel and arrival.

The city gradually takes shape in Campo Santo Stefano, where everyday life and historical memory overlap. Children move through the square, coffee is served at café tables, and poetry mingles with the symbols of religion. Yet darker images intrude: traces of blood and anarchist graffiti disturb the beauty of the scene, suggesting conflict beneath Venice’s elegant surface.

Elsewhere, an Istrian refugee searches the shoreline for nails and pieces of driftwood. From the debris carried across the Adriatic, he attempts to build a makeshift gondola. His fragile craft becomes an emblem of exile and survival—a home, a vessel, and a future assembled from what history has discarded.

Music and the splendor of imperial wealth deepen the city’s dreamlike atmosphere, but they cannot conceal its legacy of suffering. In the Palazzo Ducale, visions of power and pain merge around the figure of an old man who remains bound yet continues to paint waves. His persistence transforms art into an act of resistance: although confined by violence, memory, or history, he keeps imagining movement and freedom.
outputs.L4:
The poem presents Venice through the fragmented perspective of a traveler moving between airports, canals, streets, artworks, and memories. Rather than offering a stable portrait of the city, it assembles brief sensory impressions: water, stone, voices, crowds, children, refugees, and traces of former empires. These images reproduce the disorientation of travel and displacement. The speaker seems to occupy an uncertain position—both visitor and witness—trying to understand a place whose visible beauty cannot be separated from the histories buried beneath it.

Memory in the poem is not orderly or private. It moves unpredictably between personal experience and collective history, allowing the present to become entangled with earlier migrations, wars, conquests, and exiles. Airports and other transitional spaces emphasize this instability. They are places of arrival and departure, but also of waiting, surveillance, and separation. The traveler’s movement therefore echoes the more desperate journeys of refugees, creating a contrast between voluntary travel and forced displacement. By placing these experiences near one another, the poem draws attention to the unequal conditions under which people cross borders.

Venice itself appears as a city made of layers. Its canals, architecture, and art evoke elegance and cultural achievement, yet they also preserve evidence of trade, imperial ambition, religious conflict, and exploitation. The city’s celebrated beauty is inseparable from the wealth and violence that produced it. Images of decay—crumbling buildings, damaged surfaces, darkened water, or the general sense of a civilization fading—suggest that imperial power never disappears completely. Instead, it survives in monuments, institutions, inherited inequalities, and cultural memory.

The figures of refugees and children intensify the poem’s concern with vulnerability. Children may represent innocence, continuity, or the possibility of a future, but their presence also makes the surrounding suffering more disturbing. Refugees, meanwhile, embody the consequences of political violence and historical upheaval. They are not presented as distant abstractions; their proximity interrupts the traveler’s aesthetic experience of Venice. The poem refuses to allow art, tourism, or picturesque scenery to conceal the realities of dispossession.

Its fragmented form is central to this effect. The rapid shifts between locations, people, and historical references prevent the reader from settling into a single interpretation. This movement resembles the workings of memory, in which sensations awaken unrelated or partially connected images. It also reflects the experience of exile, where identity and place can feel broken into pieces. The poem’s discontinuities therefore do not merely create confusion; they reveal how the past intrudes upon the present and how individual perception is shaped by histories that may be only partly understood.

Ultimately, the poem portrays beauty and suffering as inseparable. Venice is at once enchanting and decaying, a destination and a crossroads, a work of art and a monument to power. The traveler’s observations show that the city cannot be viewed innocently: every canal, painting, child, and ruined surface carries echoes of movement, loss, violence, and survival. By bringing these elements together, the poem suggests that the present remains haunted by exile and imperial history. Venice becomes not only a physical city but also a symbol of the burden of memory—a place where splendor endures, even as the suffering on which it was built continues to demand recognition.
outputs.L5:
**And, The, Still**

And the world kept turning, though no one seemed to notice. The rain softened, the streets emptied, and the last train disappeared into the night.

Still, one window remained lit.

Behind it, an old man sat beside a silent telephone, holding a photograph worn pale by time. The clock moved forward. The memories did not.

And then, just before dawn, the telephone rang.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a lyrical free-verse poem about arriving exhausted in Venice through Marco Polo Airport, blending summer heat, Campo Santo Stefano, anarchist graffiti, refugees, children, and the fading grandeur of empire.
counterfactuals.output:
We arrive emptied of sleep  
at Marco Polo Airport,  
the name already a map of longing—  
glass doors breathing us  
into the white furnace of July.

Beyond the runway, the lagoon  
holds its tarnished mirror.  
Boats shoulder the heat;  
water taxis scatter coins of light,  
and Venice rises slowly,  
a fever dream built on timber,  
salt, and command.

By Campo Santo Stefano  
our bags have grown heavier  
than our histories.  
Cafés bloom beneath awnings,  
pigeons stagger through shadow,  
and children chase a red ball  
across stones polished  
by centuries of leaving.

On a wall, black paint insists:  
NO GODS, NO MASTERS—  
the letters running  
as if the city itself were sweating.  
Nearby, another hand has written  
BORDERS KILL,  
and the words flare briefly  
under the indifferent sun.

At the vaporetto stop,  
refugee families wait  
with plastic folders, quiet bundles,  
children asleep against their knees.  
The lagoon rocks every language  
without asking for papers.  
A little girl trails her fingers  
through the green water,  
drawing a country  
that vanishes as she makes it.

All afternoon the palaces  
shed their faded colors—  
rose, ocher, drowned gold—  
facades keeping the posture of empire  
while plaster loosens  
grain by grain.

Lions still lift stone wings  
over doorways.  
Saints still stare from niches.  
But the sea has entered everything:  
the marble, the hinges,  
the ledgers of conquest,  
the names of merchants  
who mistook distance for possession.

Exhaustion makes prophets of us.  
We see how beauty survives  
not by remaining whole  
but by leaning—  
balcony toward canal,  
stranger toward stranger,  
the old world toward the tide.

Evening cools Campo Santo Stefano.  
Children call to one another  
between bells.  
The graffiti darkens.  
A woman unfolds bread  
and passes it down the bench.

Above us, windows kindle  
one by one,  
small republics of light.

And Venice, exhausted too,  
lets its grandeur fade  
without surrendering its shimmer—  
an empire becoming water,  
a city becoming welcome,  
the night arriving by boat.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a surreal prose poem set in Venice that moves associatively between an airport, a water taxi, an Internet café, a church, the Adriatic refugee crisis, and an old painter working inside the Palazzo Ducale.
counterfactuals.output:
At Marco Polo Airport, the departures board fluttered like a cage of black birds, each city briefly pecking through the dark: Tunis, Vienna, Damascus, erased. My suitcase circled without arriving. Beyond the glass, Venice waited in its drowned arithmetic, adding one canal to another until the sum became sky.

A water taxi took me into the blue mouth of morning. The driver wore a red scarf and spoke to no one, though now and then he nodded toward the empty seat beside him, where a small salt-stiffened jacket lay folded. The lagoon slapped the hull with a passport it could not stamp. Islands passed like thoughts abandoned halfway: cemetery, bell tower, warehouse, cloud.

At an Internet café near San Zaccaria, the screens glowed in their little aquariums. I paid for twenty minutes and watched the Adriatic refresh itself: a map of arrows, a photograph of an orange boat crowded beyond counting, the word *rescued*, the word *missing*, both blinking beneath an advertisement for cheap rooms. Outside, tourists lifted cones of gelato to their mouths. Inside, the printer began producing wet pages, each bearing the face of the sea.

I followed them into a church.

There, candles stood in rows like a harbor at night. A marble saint had tilted his ear toward the floor, listening for engines under the stones. I placed no coin in the box, yet a flame opened. In its center, a mother held a child above the waves; in the child’s fist was an airport luggage tag; on the tag, in careful ink, someone had written: **VENICE, IF POSSIBLE**.

The church door swung wide and the nave became the Sala del Maggior Consiglio. Inside the Palazzo Ducale, an old painter balanced on a scaffold beneath Tintoretto’s thunder. He had been restoring *Paradise* for so long that his beard contained scaffolds of its own. With a brush made from gull feathers, he painted tiny boats among the angels.

“Those were not there,” I said.

“They were always there,” he answered, dipping his brush into a cup of Adriatic water. “Paradise is crowded at the edges.”

He painted an airport runway across a saint’s palm, an Internet cursor into the eye of God, a water taxi carrying the dead and the living under the Bridge of Sighs. Each time his brush touched the wall, somewhere a screen went dark; somewhere a life jacket filled with wind; somewhere a name crossed the sea without its body.

By evening, Venice had put on her mask of windows. The old painter descended, leaving one square of heaven unfinished. Through it came the sound of propellers, bells, keyboards, waves—the city’s many languages trying to pronounce mercy.

Then the lagoon rose quietly into the palace and lifted us all: painter, saints, tourists, refugees, the silent taxi driver, my unclaimed suitcase. We floated beneath the gilded ceiling, weightless as destinations.

Only the small jacket remained below, folded on the marble floor.

In the morning, it had become a door.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a modernist travel poem in the style of fragmented memory. Include the dog days of summer, crickets in a black walnut tree, Saint Stephen, a child playing hopscotch, music drifting from an academy, and images of Venice’s violent history.
counterfactuals.output:
**Vespers, with Departures**

The train forgot us  
somewhere after noon—  
rails whitening under the dog days of summer,  
heat laid flat across the fields  
like a map no empire could fold.

In the black walnut tree  
the crickets kept their iron counsel.  
Minute teeth. Blind clocks.  
I remembered—or invented—  
your hand at the station window.

Saint Stephen stood in a roadside chapel,  
stones gathered forever in his robe,  
his gold halo blistered by weather.  
Someone had left wildflowers  
in a petrol can.

Chalk struck pavement:

  one square, two—  
  the child lifted on one foot  
  over earth, over heaven,  
  over the small numbered graves  
  of hopscotch.

From the academy, music drifted—  
scales loosening into evening,  
a violin repeating the blue mistake  
of distance. Each note crossed the canal  
and returned without its name.

Venice: beautiful wound.

Under the winged lion,  
oars once blackened the lagoons;  
the Arsenal hammered fleets from timber,  
galleys went east with merchants and knives.  
There were masks for plague,  
marble steps washed clean of blood,  
heads displayed between columns  
where tourists now photograph the dusk.

I saw Saint Mark’s horses  
remembering theft,  
bronze mouths open toward Constantinople.  
I saw red banners rise and fall  
inside the water’s broken mirror.

Or perhaps only laundry moved  
above a narrow street.

Night came in fragments:  
walnut leaves, chalk dust, bells,  
the academy’s final chord  
caught under a bridge.

The child had gone home.  
The crickets continued.

And summer—old accomplice—  
pressed its hot thumb  
against every vanishing thing.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Imagine a weary American poet visiting Venice in oppressive heat. Write a single dense stanza in which ordinary observations—black coffee, children’s voices, graffiti, driftwood, and a dog—open into meditations on exile, art, empire, and suffering.
counterfactuals.output: Black coffee cooling to tar beneath the awning, while children’s voices rise from the alley like bright coins flung against a shutter, I read the graffiti bleeding through imperial plaster—names, obscenities, one crooked heart—and think how every exile learns the empire first as weather: this heat pressing its wet thumb to the eyes, these palaces afloat on labor, plague, and salt; along the fondamenta a rib of driftwood knocks and knocks, petitioning the stone to remember the forest, while a yellow dog sleeps beneath Tintoretto’s saints, untroubled by beauty or its price, and I, American, tired heir to distances, wars, museums, stand holding my bitter cup as if it were the last dark fact, hearing the children vanish over a bridge and wondering whether art is mercy, or merely suffering taught to sing where power can overhear it.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an evocative, dreamlike poem titled “Anarchia è ordine,” set around Campo Santo Stefano and the Venetian lagoon, featuring an Istrian refugee building a gondola from debris and an aged captive painting waves in the Doge’s Palace.
counterfactuals.output:
# Anarchia è ordine

At Campo Santo Stefano, dawn loosens  
its pale ribbons from the chimneys.  
Pigeons turn like ash above the stones,  
and every shutter dreams in green.

An Istrian refugee kneels by the canal,  
his pockets full of lost addresses.  
From splintered doors, a broken oar,  
the ribs of chairs drowned years ago,  
he builds a gondola.

He nails the fog to its black hull.  
He binds each seam with strands of seaweed,  
whispering the names of vanished villages  
until the wood remembers forests.

Across the lagoon, the islands drift—  
bells without towers, gardens under salt.  
Murano burns inside a cloud;  
San Giorgio is a sleeping animal  
with moonlight breathing through its teeth.

In the Doge’s Palace, behind a wall  
where footsteps pass like distant rain,  
an aged captive paints the waves.  
He has forgotten the horizon,  
so he invents it: ultramarine,  
verdigris, the white of a gull’s cry.

Night after night, his painted water rises,  
flooding councils, crowns, and verdicts.  
The lions swim out of their books.  
Gold frames open like windows.  
The judges’ masks fill slowly with fish.

At last the refugee pushes off  
from Campo Santo Stefano.  
His gondola, made of wreckage,  
floats more lightly than a promise.

Beneath the Bridge of Sighs he passes,  
and the captive hears the oar  
divide the darkness into silver.

Neither man speaks.  
The lagoon speaks for them—  
in broken timber, in painted foam,  
in borders washed from every map.

On the palace wall, one sentence flowers  
through plaster, salt, and sleep:

**Anarchia è ordine—**

and Venice, upside down in the water,  
believes it.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
